# Proteomics {#sec-proteomics}

::: {.callout-note title="From the exam description"}
Different proteomics methods. How are these used, algorithms.
:::

## Introduction

Proteomics studies the proteins themselves: which ones are present, how
abundant they are, how they are modified and whom they interact with. mRNA
levels are only moderately correlated with protein levels, and many
regulatory events, such as phosphorylation, cleavage and complex
formation, happen only at the protein level. Proteomics therefore
provides information that genomics and transcriptomics cannot
[@aebersold2003; @aebersold2016].

Most proteomics today is done with **mass spectrometry (MS)**. In
*bottom-up* or *shotgun* proteomics, proteins are digested with trypsin.
The peptides are separated by liquid chromatography, ionised and measured
in the mass spectrometer (MS1). Selected peptides are then fragmented and
the fragments are measured as well (MS2, tandem MS). Fragmentation mostly
breaks the peptide backbone, giving series of b- and y-ions whose mass
differences correspond to amino acids. The central computational task is
to work out which peptide produced each spectrum. Database search engines
such as SEQUEST and Mascot compare each experimental spectrum with
theoretical spectra of all candidate peptides from a protein database and
score the best peptide-spectrum match (PSM) [@eng1994; @perkins1999].
Alternatives include matching against libraries of previously observed
spectra and de novo sequencing. Deep learning now predicts fragment
spectra and retention times accurately [@gessulat2019].

Because every spectrum gets a best match, error control is essential. The
*target–decoy* strategy searches against real and reversed or shuffled
sequences together. The number of decoy hits estimates the number of
false target hits, and hence the false discovery rate
[@elias2007; @nesvizhskii2010]. Machine-learning rescoring, such as
Percolator, improves the separation between correct and incorrect matches
[@kall2007]. Going from peptides to proteins adds a further problem,
*protein inference*, because many peptides are shared between related
proteins.

There are several ways to quantify proteins. These include label-free
methods based on peptide intensities, metabolic labelling (SILAC) and
isobaric chemical tags (TMT), which allow many samples to be pooled
[@cox2008]. In *data-dependent acquisition* (DDA) the instrument chooses
which peptides to fragment, so measurements are partly random and some
values are missing. *Data-independent acquisition* (DIA/SWATH) fragments
everything in wide mass windows and gives more reproducible results, at
the cost of complex, mixed spectra that need dedicated software
[@gillet2012; @ludwig2018; @demichev2020].

Large projects have produced draft maps of the human proteome
[@kim2014; @wilhelm2014]. They have been complemented by antibody-based
imaging of protein localisation in the Human Protein Atlas [@uhlen2015].
Data are shared through PRIDE and ProteomeXchange [@perezriverol2022].
MS is also central to interaction proteomics, such as affinity
purification and cross-linking, which is discussed in
@sec-protein-interactions.

## Key concepts

- Bottom-up (shotgun) vs. top-down proteomics; LC-MS/MS; fragmentation and b/y ions
- Peptide identification: database search (SEQUEST, Mascot, Andromeda), spectral libraries, de novo sequencing
- Error control: target–decoy approach, peptide-spectrum-match FDR, Percolator; the protein inference problem
- Acquisition strategies: data-dependent (DDA) vs. data-independent (DIA/SWATH) vs. targeted (SRM/PRM)
- Quantification: label-free, SILAC, isobaric tags (TMT/iTRAQ)
- Post-translational modifications (e.g. phosphoproteomics)
- Interaction proteomics (AP-MS, cross-linking MS; see @sec-protein-interactions) and structural MS
- Deep learning for spectrum and retention-time prediction
- Antibody-based proteomics: the Human Protein Atlas
- Repositories and standards: PRIDE/ProteomeXchange

## Key papers

### Reviews — start here

- @aebersold2003 — mass spectrometry-based proteomics.
- @aebersold2016 — mass-spectrometric exploration of proteome structure and function.
- @nesvizhskii2010 — computational methods and error-rate estimation for peptide and protein identification.
- @ludwig2018 — data-independent acquisition-based proteomics: a tutorial.

### Identification and error control

- @eng1994 — SEQUEST: matching spectra to sequences.
- @perkins1999 — Mascot: probability-based protein identification.
- @elias2007 — the target–decoy search strategy.
- @kall2007 — Percolator: semi-supervised learning for peptide identification.

### Quantification and acquisition

- @cox2008 — MaxQuant.
- @gillet2012 — SWATH-MS.
- @demichev2020 — DIA-NN: neural networks for DIA data.
- @gessulat2019 — Prosit: deep-learning prediction of fragment spectra.

### Proteome maps and resources

- @kim2014 — a draft map of the human proteome.
- @wilhelm2014 — mass-spectrometry-based draft of the human proteome.
- @uhlen2015 — the tissue-based map of the human proteome (Human Protein Atlas).
- @perezriverol2022 — the PRIDE database.
- @ideker2001 — integrated genomic and proteomic analysis of a perturbed network.
